evidence: ProjectController.create, UserController.create and TaskController.create/listByProject/assign each build a RequestReader and call requiredString/optionalString, so parsing goes through one abstraction.
Every controller action delegates to an injected use case's execute(...). None of them touches repositories or domain entities directly.
The create actions in ProjectController, UserController and TaskController return res.status(201).json(...). The assign, complete and list actions return res.json(...).
TaskUseCases groups createTask, listProjectTasks, assignTask and completeTask. This is a reasonable way to inject a controller with several operations.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files are HTTP controllers that do the same job. Each one parses the request through the shared RequestReader, calls application use cases, and writes the response. Input parsing lives in RequestReader, which is outside this unit, so the controllers don't duplicate it. Business rules stay in the use cases. Status codes are applied consistently: 201 for creates and 200 for the rest. TaskController injects a TaskUseCases bag while the other two inject one use case each. That fits, because TaskController has four operations, and it doesn't bypass any abstraction. No file mixes in an unrelated concern.
